**How to Count Mitochondria in a Cell** Below is a practical, step‑by‑step workflow that you can adapt to most laboratory settings. It covers the most common approaches (fluorescence microscopy, electron microscopy, and mtDNA‑copy‑number assays) and gives you a sense of the typical range of mitochondrial numbers in different cell types. | **Method** | **Key Reagents / Equipment** | **Typical Workflow** | **Pros / Cons** | **Typical Mitochondrial Count** | |------------|------------------------------|----------------------|-----------------|---------------------------------| | Fluorescence microscopy (confocal or wide‑field) | MitoTracker™ Green FM (or other mitochondrial dyes), DAPI (nucleus), 20–40× objective, image‑analysis software (ImageJ/Fiji, CellProfiler) | 1. Culture cells on glass coverslips.
2. Stain with MitoTracker (e.g., 100 nM for 30 min).
3. Wash, fix (optional), mount.
4. Acquire z‑stacks (if confocal).
5. Use thresholding + particle analysis to count mitochondria per cell. | • Fast, inexpensive.
• Can be done on live cells.
• Limited resolution (~200 nm). | 10–200 per cell (depends on cell type & metabolic state). | | Confocal microscopy with 3‑D reconstruction | Same as above + confocal microscope, 3‑D rendering (Imaris, Volocity) | Same staining; acquire full z‑stack; render 3‑D; count mitochondria manually or automatically. | • Better 3‑D accuracy.
• More time‑consuming. | 10–200 per cell. | | Super‑resolution (STED, SIM, PALM/STORM) | STED‑compatible dye (e.g., MitoTracker‑Red), SIM or PALM/STORM setup | Stain, image at <100 nm resolution, count mitochondria. | • Highest resolution; can resolve individual cristae.
• Requires specialized equipment. | 10–200 per cell. | | Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) | Fixation (glutaraldehyde + osmium tetroxide), resin embedding, ultrathin sectioning, TEM | 1. Fix cells.
2. Embed, section (70 nm).
3. Image at 80–120 kV.
4. Count mitochondria in each section; extrapolate to whole cell. | • Gold standard for ultrastructure.
• Labor‑intensive, low throughput. | 10–200 per cell (exact numbers depend on section thickness). | | Cryo‑electron tomography (cryo‑ET) | Cryo‑plunge freezing, cryo‑TEM, tomography software | 1. Freeze cells rapidly.
2. Collect tilt series.
3. Reconstruct 3‑D volume.
4. Count mitochondria. | • Near‑native state, 3‑D detail.
• Very low throughput. | 10–200 per cell. | | Flow cytometry (mitochondrial mass) | MitoTracker Green, flow cytometer, gating strategy | 1. Stain cells.
2. Run flow cytometer.
3. Measure mean fluorescence intensity (MFI) as proxy for mitochondrial mass. | • High throughput.
• Does not give absolute count; only relative mass. | – | | mtDNA copy‑number by qPCR / ddPCR | Primers for MT‑ND1 (mtDNA) and nuclear reference (e.g., β‑actin), qPCR machine or ddPCR system | 1. Extract total DNA.
2. Perform qPCR/ddPCR.
3. Calculate mtDNA/nuclear DNA ratio → copy number per cell. | • Indirect measure; assumes one mitochondrion per mtDNA copy.
• Sensitive, quantitative. | 100–10 000 copies per cell (depends on cell type). | | Proteomics (mitochondrial protein abundance) | Mass spectrometry, mitochondrial isolation, label‑free quantification | 1. Isolate mitochondria.
2. Digest proteins.
3. LC‑MS/MS.
4. Quantify mitochondrial proteins. | • Provides functional context.
• Requires specialized equipment. | – | --- ### Practical Tips 1. **Cell Type Matters** - **Neurons**: ~200–500 mitochondria per axon segment. - **Myocytes**: ~200–400 per sarcomere. - **Fibroblasts**: ~10–50 per cell. - **Cancer cells**: Often 50–200, but can be higher if highly glycolytic. 2. **Staining Conditions** - Avoid over‑staining; high dye concentrations can cause aggregation. - For live‑cell imaging, keep dye concentration ≤ 200 nM and incubation ≤ 30 min. 3. **Image Analysis** - Use a consistent threshold across all images. - Apply size filters to exclude debris (< 0.2 µm²). - For 3‑D stacks, use “Analyze Particles” in 3‑D mode or Imaris “Spot” detection. 4. **Counting Accuracy** - In TEM, count mitochondria in multiple serial sections and use stereological corrections (e.g., Abercrombie correction). - In fluorescence, consider that overlapping mitochondria may be counted as one; use deconvolution or 3‑D rendering to mitigate. 5. **Controls** - Include a known cell line with established mitochondrial count (e.g., HeLa cells). - Run a negative control (no dye) to assess background. --- ### Quick Reference Protocol (Fluorescence Counting) ```text 1. Plate 1×10⁵ cells per 12‑mm coverslip in 24‑well plate. 2. Incubate 24 h at 37 °C, 5% CO₂. 3. Prepare MitoTracker Green: 100 nM in PBS. 4. Add dye to cells, incubate 30 min at 37 °C. 5. Wash 3× with PBS. 6. (Optional) Fix with 4% paraformaldehyde for 10 min. 7. Mount with ProLong Gold (with DAPI). 8. Image with 20× objective, 512×512 pixels, 2–3 µm z‑step. 9. In Fiji: Image → Stacks → Z Project (max intensity). 10. Process: Image → Adjust → Threshold (Otsu). 11. Analyze → Analyze Particles: size 0.2–5 µm², circularity 0.5–1.0. 12. Record particle count per cell; average over ≥ 30 cells. ``` --- ### Typical Numbers (Illustrative) | Cell Type | Mitochondria per Cell | Notes | |-----------|-----------------------|-------| | HeLa | 50–150 | Highly proliferative, moderate metabolism | | NIH‑3T3 | 20–60 | Fibroblast, moderate energy demand | | C2C12 (myoblast) | 30–80 | Muscle precursor | | Primary neurons | 200–500 (per axon segment) | High energy demand | | HepG2 (liver) | 50–120 | Metabolic hub | | Cancer (highly glycolytic) | 100–300 | Variable | --- ### Bottom Line - **Fluorescence microscopy** is the most accessible method for routine counting. - **TEM** gives the most accurate structural count but is low throughput. - **mtDNA copy‑number assays** provide an indirect but quantitative estimate of mitochondrial abundance. Choose the method that best fits your resources, required resolution, and throughput needs. If you need a quick estimate, start with MitoTracker staining and automated particle counting in Fiji. If you require precise ultrastructural data, move to TEM or cryo‑ET.
